title: Stone Steps and Grass Bridges of the Andes

passage.title: Stone Steps and Grass Bridges of the Andes
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Passage
passage.text:
Five hundred years ago, the Inca Empire stretched for two thousand miles along the spine of the Andes Mountains in South America. This high world of jagged peaks and deep river gorges was one of the hardest places on Earth to build a kingdom. Flat farmland barely existed on the steep cliffs. Heavy summer rains could quickly wash away loose dirt. At night, icy mountain winds dropped temperatures below freezing and threatened to kill young crops. Yet Inca engineers solved both farming and travel challenges using local stone and wild mountain grass.

To create flat fields on steep slopes, workers carved giant steps called terraces into the mountainside. Each step was held in place by a slanted wall of tightly fitted granite blocks. Beneath the rich topsoil of every terrace, layers of coarse river gravel and packed sand were carefully arranged by Inca masons. When fierce storms drenched the peaks, this underground filter let extra water drain safely to the step below so the soil could not erode. Even better, the dark stone walls soaked up warm sunlight all afternoon. Throughout the freezing night, the rocks retained that stored heat and kept potato and corn roots from turning to ice.

Growing food was only half the battle across the broken mountain chain. The Inca also needed to connect their royal road network across roaring canyons that were hundreds of feet deep. Because the Andes lacked tall, straight timber trees for wooden beams, stone arches were too heavy to cross such wide gaps. Instead, engineers turned to tough golden grass that grew wild on the high plains.

Every year, whole villages gathered to twist millions of pliable grass stems into cords as thick as a person's waist. Workers braided three or four of these giant cables together to form the floor and hand ropes of a suspension bridge. They anchored the ends around heavy stone piers on each cliff edge. Some grass bridges spanned gorges more than one hundred fifty feet wide.

Although grass rots over time in rain and wind, the Inca turned that weakness into a yearly tradition. Each spring, local communities wove fresh cables and replaced the old bridge in just three days. While stone terraces conquered the steep slopes, woven grass bridges linked the empire together across the sky.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 2:

"Beneath the rich topsoil of every terrace, layers of coarse river gravel and packed sand were carefully arranged by Inca masons."

Based on the structure of this sentence, who or what performed the action of arranging?

options.text: Layers of coarse river gravel and packed sand
options.childFeedback: The layers of coarse river gravel and packed sand are the materials being put in place, not the workers doing the arranging.

options.text: The rich topsoil at the top of every terrace
options.childFeedback: The rich topsoil sat above the gravel and sand layers; soil cannot arrange stones beneath itself.

options.text: Inca masons building the mountain terraces
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 2, the phrase 'were carefully arranged by Inca masons' tells us that the Inca masons performed the action of arranging the gravel and sand layers.

options.text: Fierce summer storms drenching the mountain peaks
options.childFeedback: Fierce summer storms drenched the peaks later on, while the underground gravel filter had already been built by Inca masons.

questions.provingSentenceText: Beneath the rich topsoil of every terrace, layers of coarse river gravel and packed sand were carefully arranged by Inca masons.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 2, the phrase 'were carefully arranged by Inca masons' tells us that the Inca masons performed the action of arranging the gravel and sand layers.
questions.parentExplanation: In this passive sentence, 'layers of coarse river gravel and packed sand' is the grammatical subject receiving the action. The true actor performing the arranging is in the final 'by' phrase: 'Inca masons' (Option C).
questions.retryHint: Look at the end of the sentence in Paragraph 2 after 'arranged by' to see who put the gravel and sand layers in place.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 2:

"Throughout the freezing night, the rocks retained that stored heat and kept potato and corn roots from turning to ice."

What does the word "retained" mean as it is used in this sentence?

options.text: Held on to and kept inside
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 2, 'retained' means held on to and kept inside, because the dark stone walls soaked up warm sunlight all afternoon and held that heat through the freezing night.

options.text: Blocked sunlight from reaching the stone walls
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 2 says the dark stone walls soaked up warm sunlight all afternoon rather than blocking it, and then held that warmth at night.

options.text: Cracked into small pieces of river gravel
options.childFeedback: The tightly fitted granite walls stayed solid to hold the terrace steps in place; they did not crack into gravel at night.

options.text: Melted the granite blocks into liquid rock
options.childFeedback: Afternoon sunshine only warmed the granite stones enough to keep crop roots from freezing; it could never melt rock into liquid.

questions.provingSentenceText: Throughout the freezing night, the rocks retained that stored heat and kept potato and corn roots from turning to ice.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 2, 'retained' means held on to and kept inside, because the dark stone walls soaked up warm sunlight all afternoon and held that heat through the freezing night.
questions.parentExplanation: The root 'tenere' means to hold ('re-' + 'tain' = hold back/keep). Because the stone walls soaked up afternoon sun and kept crop roots from freezing overnight, 'retained' means held on to that stored heat (Option A).
questions.retryHint: Read the sentence right before this one in Paragraph 2 to see what the dark stone walls soaked up all afternoon and kept at night.

questions.prompt: According to Paragraph 3, why did Inca engineers weave bridges out of wild mountain grass instead of building them from wood or stone?

options.text: Wooden bridges attracted herds of wild animals that ate the corn and potato crops.
options.childFeedback: The passage never mentions wooden bridges attracting wild animals to eat crops; the problem was a lack of tall, straight timber trees.

options.text: Inca masons did not know how to carve or fit granite blocks together on steep cliffs.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 2 proves that Inca masons were experts at carving and fitting granite blocks together on steep mountain cliffs.

options.text: Wild mountain grass never rotted in the rain and lasted for hundreds of years without repairs.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 5 actually states the opposite: grass rots over time in rain and wind, so villagers wove fresh bridge cables every spring.

options.text: The high Andes lacked tall, straight trees for wooden beams, and stone arches were too heavy to cross such wide canyons.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 3 states that the high Andes lacked tall, straight timber trees for wooden beams and that stone arches were too heavy to stretch across such wide canyons.

questions.provingSentenceText: Because the Andes lacked tall, straight timber trees for wooden beams, stone arches were too heavy to cross such wide gaps.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 3 states that the high Andes lacked tall, straight timber trees for wooden beams and that stone arches were too heavy to stretch across such wide canyons.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 3 directly explains the material constraint: 'Because the Andes lacked tall, straight timber trees for wooden beams, stone arches were too heavy to cross such wide gaps,' leading engineers to use wild golden grass (Option D).
questions.retryHint: Check the third sentence of Paragraph 3 for the two reasons why wooden beams and stone arches wouldn't work across deep Andean canyons.

questions.prompt: How does the author organize the information across the entire passage?

options.text: By focusing only on how villagers braided three or four grass cables together to form a single bridge floor
options.childFeedback: Braiding grass cables for bridges is only covered in Paragraphs 4 and 5, leaving out the stone farming terraces in Paragraph 2.

options.text: By comparing the height of the Andes Mountains to other mountain ranges in North America and Europe
options.childFeedback: The passage never compares the Andes Mountains to ranges in North America or Europe; it stays focused on Inca engineering in South America.

options.text: By introducing the harsh mountain challenges of the Andes and then explaining the engineering solutions the Inca created for farming and travel
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 1 introduces the steep cliffs, heavy rains, and freezing nights of the Andes, and Paragraphs 2–5 explain how Inca engineers solved farming with stone terraces and travel with grass bridges.

options.text: By arguing that woven grass bridges were much more important to the Inca Empire than stone farming terraces
options.childFeedback: The author presents both stone terraces and grass bridges as equally vital partners ('Growing food was only half the battle'), not one as more important.

questions.provingSentenceText: Yet Inca engineers solved both farming and travel challenges using local stone and wild mountain grass.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 1 introduces the steep cliffs, heavy rains, and freezing nights of the Andes, and Paragraphs 2–5 explain how Inca engineers solved farming with stone terraces and travel with grass bridges.
questions.parentExplanation: Aligned to ELAGSE5RI5, the passage uses a clear Problem/Solution structure forecast in Paragraph 1 ('solved both farming and travel challenges'): Paragraph 2 details the terrace solution for farming, and Paragraphs 3–5 detail the suspension bridge solution for travel (Option C).
questions.retryHint: Look at the last sentence of Paragraph 1 and the last sentence of Paragraph 5 to see how the author pairs farming and travel challenges with Inca solutions.

questions.prompt: PART A: Based on Paragraph 2, how did the underground layers of gravel and sand protect the Inca farming terraces?

options.text: They allowed heavy storm water to drain safely to lower steps so the rich topsoil would not wash down the mountain.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 2 explains that the underground layers of gravel and sand acted as a filter during fierce storms, letting extra water drain safely to lower steps so the topsoil would not wash away.

options.text: They absorbed afternoon sunlight and warmed the potato roots during freezing mountain nights.
options.childFeedback: It was the dark granite walls on the outside of the terraces—not the buried gravel underneath—that soaked up afternoon sunlight and held heat at night.

options.text: They provided a soft place for villagers to anchor the ends of their woven grass bridge cables.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 4 says villagers anchored grass bridge cables around heavy stone piers on cliff edges, not in the gravel under farming topsoil.

options.text: They stopped all rain clouds from forming above the peaks of the Andes Mountains.
options.childFeedback: Layers of gravel buried beneath the dirt helped drain rainwater after storms hit, but they could not stop rain clouds from forming in the sky.

questions.provingSentenceText: When fierce storms drenched the peaks, this underground filter let extra water drain safely to the step below so the soil could not erode.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 2 explains that the underground layers of gravel and sand acted as a filter during fierce storms, letting extra water drain safely to lower steps so the topsoil would not wash away.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 2 describes two distinct features of the terraces: the underground gravel/sand filter drained storm water so soil would not erode (Option A), whereas the dark granite walls stored solar heat (Option B, a Syntactic/Concept Reversal trap).
questions.retryHint: Read the fourth sentence of Paragraph 2 to see what the 'underground filter' of gravel and sand did when fierce storms drenched the peaks.

questions.prompt: PART B: Which quotation from the passage best supports the correct answer to Question 5?

options.text: "Flat farmland barely existed on the steep cliffs."
options.childFeedback: This detail from Paragraph 1 only states the problem of steep cliffs having little flat land, not how the underground gravel layers worked.

options.text: "When fierce storms drenched the peaks, this underground filter let extra water drain safely to the step below so the soil could not erode."
options.childFeedback: This quotation from Paragraph 2 directly supports Question 5 by explaining how the underground filter of gravel and sand let storm water drain safely so the soil could not erode.

options.text: "Even better, the dark stone walls soaked up warm sunlight all afternoon."
options.childFeedback: This sentence from Paragraph 2 explains how the outer stone walls absorbed heat, rather than how the buried gravel and sand drained storm water.

options.text: "Each spring, local communities wove fresh cables and replaced the old bridge in just three days."
options.childFeedback: This line from Paragraph 5 describes replacing woven grass bridges each spring, which has nothing to do with terrace drainage in Paragraph 2.

questions.provingSentenceText: When fierce storms drenched the peaks, this underground filter let extra water drain safely to the step below so the soil could not erode.
questions.childTip: This quotation from Paragraph 2 directly supports Question 5 by explaining how the underground filter of gravel and sand let storm water drain safely so the soil could not erode.
questions.parentExplanation: Option B directly proves the claim in Part A by quoting how the underground gravel and sand filter drained storm water safely so the topsoil could not erode.
questions.retryHint: Look for the quote from Paragraph 2 that mentions the 'underground filter' and what it prevented during storms.
